system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2140-01-29 16:17:00 to 2140-01-30 16:54:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can I start by confirming your name?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m Mary. I’ve been feeling really sick the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. You came in with nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about when it started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started about three days ago. I ate two slices of cheese pizza, and within an hour, I started vomiting. Then the diarrhea came.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did anyone else eat the pizza or get sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, just me. But I do have chronic pancreatitis, and my doctor said this kind of reaction can happen if I eat fatty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. The pizza was probably a trigger. You mentioned you take Creon with meals—were you able to take it that day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took it, but I threw up soon after. I haven’t eaten anything since yesterday noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And how’s the nausea now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better since I got the IV medicine in the ER. But I still feel bloated and tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you got Reglan and fluids in the ER. We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now and start you on clear liquids to see how you tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been using Zofran at home, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your Zofran and monitor you. We also checked your blood work and lipase—good news, your pancreas isn’t flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But why the greasy, pale stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely due to your pancreatic insufficiency. When your pancreas doesn’t make enough enzymes, fat isn’t digested well, so it comes out in your stool.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So Creon should help, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll make sure you’re taking it correctly and increase the dose if needed once you’re eating again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I’ve also been dizzy when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s probably from dehydration. We’re giving you fluids through the IV, so that should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also have this rash under my breasts and in my groin. It’s been itching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I saw that on exam. It looks like a yeast infection, which can happen more easily with your glucose intolerance. We’ll keep you on the Nystatin cream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using it for a couple days. Is it safe to keep using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe and appropriate. Just apply it twice a day as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my muscles have been aching for months. Could it be from my cholesterol medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on simvastatin. We checked your muscle enzyme levels—your CK—and it’s normal. But we’ll discuss with your primary doctor whether to adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I just don’t want to keep hurting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure your follow-up includes that. For now, we’re focused on getting your stomach settled and rehydrating you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some ginger ale last night and didn’t throw up. No diarrhea since yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re going to advance your diet to full liquids this morning and, if you do well, to a regular diet by lunch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have something light, like toast?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start with low-fat foods. Remember to take your Creon even with small meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned my lesson about pizza.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It happens. The important thing is knowing your triggers and managing them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with breakfast. No nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None. I even had a formed bowel movement this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s a good sign your gut is settling. We also got your stool test results back—no infection like C. diff or salmonella.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it really was just the pancreatitis acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks that way. No signs of infection, and your labs are stable. We’re going to discharge you today if you keep doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have persistent nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dizziness, or fever over 101. And keep avoiding fatty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications—any changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with the same meds. We lowered your valsartan dose slightly because your blood pressure was a bit high yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, keep using the Nystatin for the rash and take your Creon with every meal. Your primary doctor will follow up on your muscle aches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can go home in a couple of hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I just want to rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Take it easy, stay hydrated, and eat small, low-fat meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Feel better soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old woman was admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea following consumption of cheese pizza, in the setting of chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic insufficiency. She presented with dehydration and symptoms consistent with fat malabsorption, including greasy, pale stools. Initial management included IV fluids, anti-nausea medication, and a clear liquid diet. Her symptoms improved rapidly, with resolution of vomiting and diarrhea by the next morning. She advanced to a regular diet without complications. Stool studies ruled out infectious causes including C. difficile, Salmonella, and Giardia. Her chronic conditions, including yeast infection, myalgias, and hypertension, were managed supportively. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to avoid fatty foods, continue Creon with meals, and follow up with her primary doctor regarding persistent muscle aches.
